Muallaqat.title: The Seven Mu'allaqat
Muallaqat.lede: Seven odes once hung upon the drapes of the Kaaba — here they hang again.
Muallaqat.legend: It is told that the Arabs chose the finest odes, wrote them in gold, and hung them upon the Kaaba, so they were called the Mu'allaqat — the Suspended Ones. Each ode hangs here as an illuminated panel that unfurls as you approach.

About.title: About مُعلّقات
About.lead: مُعلّقات is a living diwan — a son's gift to his father: the Lebanese writer, novelist and translator Awad Shaaban (Beirut, 1931–2025). It gathers the finest of Arabic literature — the Muʿallaqāt, the odes, prose, and invective — in faith to his creed: "Writing is not merely talent; it is a responsibility toward the word and toward humanity."
About.collectionBody: A curated collection spanning the five eras — Jahili, Umayyad, Abbasid, Andalusi, and Modern — that presents each poet as a human being, not a name in an index. It is not an exhaustive survey of all that was ever said, but a rich beginning, meant to grow.
About.sourcingBody: Every classical text here is published verbatim, after being cross-checked against no fewer than two reputable public-domain sources (Arabic Wikisource, al-Diwan, Poets Gate, and others) that agree on the consonantal text and the order of words and verses. For the Seven Muʿallaqāt, the recension of al-Zawzanī is our tiebreaker. Vocalization is best-effort; the consonantal text and its order are the standard we hold to.
About.integrityBody: Classical works are in the public domain and are published in full, with attribution. Works by modern authors still under copyright are not hosted in full; we present only brief fair-use excerpts or links to their authorized sources. The father's own writings appear only as his family permits. Every text carries its source.
About.creditsBody: This diwan inherits its palette and type from Awad Shaaban's own site (awadshaaban.com): the cream, ink, and gold, and the self-hosted Amiri, Cairo, and Reem Kufi typefaces. It is built with Next.js, Tailwind, and next-intl, Arabic-first and right-to-left.
